issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
Kavi Perera was forty-one when the convoy was ambushed near Kandahar in 2002. He had been flying transport helicopters for the Australian Defence Force for eight years by then, and he had come to understand the work as a kind of calling—moving supplies, moving people, moving hope into places where it was needed. The morning of the attack, he was waiting on the tarmac for clearance, the rotors already turning, when the radio crackled with a request for emergency extraction from a forward operating base. Three soldiers had been hit. He lifted off without hesitation. The landing zone was chaos. Dust everywhere, the smell of cordite and something else—something burnt that he would later learn was human tissue. One of the injured men was conscious, his uniform soaked through with blood, and as Kavi's crew loaded him aboard, the man's hand—cold, trembling—grabbed Kavi's wrist. The texture of it stays with him still: the particular roughness of a field dressing soaked through, the specific way a dying man's grip feels when he is trying not to let go of the world. They got airborne. They did not make it to the hospital. The man died in the cabin while Kavi was flying, and for the last thirty seconds of that flight, Kavi had felt the weight of that hand on his wrist even though someone had already pried the fingers away. He had felt the man's blood cooling against his skin. In the years that followed, Kavi would learn to live with the memory as though it belonged to someone else entirely—a different man in a different life, someone he could observe from a distance but never quite become again. Yet when that memory surfaced, which it did without warning and without mercy, it carried the full weight of the original terror, as if twenty-two years had collapsed into nothing.

Now, at sixty-three, Kavi flies for a major American carrier as a captain on long-haul routes, a position he has held for the last decade. He and his wife Margaret live in Portland, and to anyone watching him move through an airport or into the cockpit, he appears composed—professional, even. But something fundamental has shifted inside him, something he cannot quite name but recognizes with a kind of dread. There is something wrong with him as a person. Not just in how he thinks or remembers, but in the core of who he is. He has come to understand that the man who volunteered for that extraction mission—the man who believed in purpose, who laughed easily, who moved through the world with a kind of open trust—that man no longer exists. When he looks back at photographs from before 2002, he sees a stranger, and what strikes him most is that the person in those images looks happy. Genuinely happy. He cannot reconcile that face with the man he is now. He is always miserable, he has come to believe about himself—not in dramatic moments, but in the texture of ordinary days. He moves through his marriage with Margaret as though underwater, present in body but absent in every way that matters. He used to be a happy person. He remembers that, though it feels like remembering someone else's life. Now happiness seems like a luxury reserved for people who have not seen what he has seen, people whose minds have not been permanently altered by a single moment.

The night vigilance started years ago, so gradually that he did not notice it at first. He would wake at 2:47 a.m.—the exact time the convoy was hit—and lie in the dark, listening. Margaret would be asleep beside him, and he would feel the house around him like a trap, every door and window a potential breach. He had come to believe that the world is a dangerous place—not in the abstract way that people speak of abstract dangers, but as a lived conviction that safety is an illusion that collapses the moment you stop watching. Darkness is when things become real, when the world shows its true nature. During the day, the illusion of safety holds. At night, it falls away. The scanning began during his first year with the American airline. He would enter a cockpit or a briefing room and immediately locate the exits—not consciously, but as an automatic sweep of his eyes before he could attend to anything else. His body had learned to do this without his permission. In the cabin, waiting for a flight to board, he would map the space, note where people stood, anticipate sudden movements. When a flight attendant moved too quickly, or when a passenger stood abruptly, Kavi's muscles would tense, his breath would catch in his chest. He was certain that everyone was a potential threat, though he could not articulate why. The world had shown him its teeth once, and he had never stopped waiting for them to close.

The memory itself has become something alien to him—something that belongs to a different person, a different life. When it surfaces, which it does without warning and without mercy, it carries with it the full weight of that original terror, as vivid as the moment it happened. A particular texture—canvas, or certain kinds of fabric, or even the specific roughness of the armrest in the cockpit—can trigger it instantly. The sound of a helicopter, even on television, can send him into a state where he is back on that tarmac, feeling that cold grip on his wrist. The time of day matters too. As 2:47 a.m. approaches, his body knows, and he lies awake, waiting for the moment when something inside him will fracture again. The sight of blood—even in a medical context, even in a film—can leave him shaking for hours afterward. He has come to believe that his mind is fundamentally unreliable, that the boundary between past and present has become dangerously thin, and that this defect marks him as someone who should not be trusted with the lives of three hundred passengers on every flight he captains. Margaret has noticed the changes. She has watched him become someone who is always miserable, who moves through their marriage like a man underwater. She has noticed that he no longer touches her at night, that he flinches when she reaches for him in the dark, that he sometimes calls her by the name of a crew member from a flight years ago. The airline has not noticed yet, but Kavi knows they will. He has started making mistakes, small ones, the kind that come from a mind that is never quite here. Last month, during a preflight checklist, he found himself unable to remember whether he had already verified the fuel levels, and the uncertainty terrified him in a way that no threat assessment ever could. He began a descent procedure and had to abort it halfway through because he could not recall if he had already completed it. The fear that he might one day forget something critical—that his mind might betray him in a moment that matters—has become more terrifying than any external threat. It was Margaret who finally insisted he come. She said she could not bear to watch him disappear anymore, and Kavi, sitting in the therapist's office now, can only agree. He does not know if anything can fix what he is, but he has run out of ways to hide it. What frightens him most is not that he will remember the dying soldier's grip—he will, always—but that he will forget something that costs lives, and that the defect inside him will finally be exposed for what it is: a fundamental failure of the person he has tried so hard to remain.

However, the vignette then states 'yet when that memory surfaced... as if twenty-two years had collapsed into nothing,' establishing the timeline. The critical issue is that the patient's reported age is 63, but the vignette describes the current timeframe inconsistently—it says he 'is sixty-three and now flying for a major American carrier' and 'has held for the last decade,' but then the narrative jumps between past and present in ways that obscure whether the current moment is truly when he is 63. More importantly, the vignette explicitly states he is 41 at the time of trauma and 63 at present, but the patient demographics list age as 63 with no indication this is current age. The vignette does establish approximate age context (63), so this is actually present. Upon re-review, age IS adequately reflected.
